controls.title: Ownership and accountability — named responsible role
controls.reviewer_question: Who is the named volunteer or staff member at Nourish Community Kitchen responsible and accountable for RecipeSuggest, and is this ownership clearly documented somewhere accessible to the kitchen team?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Ownership and accountability — named responsible role through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utilit
gaps: No explicit reference to training or competency requirements for the named owner in relation to AI risk awareness (aligns with GOVERN 2.2)
No mention of escalation path or reporting line above the volunteer coordinator level (executive accountability per GOVERN 2.3 is absent, though may be disproportionate at this assurance level)
No defined review cadence or trigger for reassessing ownership documentation over time
controls.gap_description: Three distinct deficiencies exist in the ownership and accountability documentation: (1) The named responsible role has no documented training or competency requirements tied to AI risk awareness — there is no evidence that the designated owner understands their obligations under an AI risk governance framework (aligned with GOVERN 2.2). (2) There is no defined escalation path or reporting line above the volunteer coordinator level, leaving executive or senior accountability unaddressed — the submission does not demonstrate how material AI risks would be escalated beyond the named role. (3) There is no defined review cadence or trigger condition for reassessing ownership documentation over time, meaning the assignment of responsibility could become stale without any mechanism to detect or correct this.
controls.gap_suggestion: Take the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase: (1) COMPETENCY — Amend the ownership policy or role description to explicitly state the minimum AI risk awareness competency expected of the named owner (e.g., completion of an AI governance or risk awareness module, or equivalent experience). Record evidence of the current owner meeting this standard. (2) ESCALATION PATH — Document a clear reporting line above the volunteer coordinator, identifying at least one senior or executive stakeholder (e.g., a board member, senior manager, or steering committee) who receives escalated AI risk issues. Even if full executive accountability is considered disproportionate at UG assurance level, a lightweight escalation contact must be named and documented. (3) REVIEW CADENCE — Insert a review schedule into the ownership documentation (e.g., annual review, or triggered by: system change, incident, or change of personnel). Record who is responsible for initiating the review and how outcomes are captured.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Documented purpose and scope — intended use and limits
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest have a written document that clearly states its intended purpose — suggesting recipes based on available ingredients for kitchen staff at Nourish Community Kitchen — and explicitly defines its limits, such as not providing nutritional advice, allergen guidance, or dietary medical recommendations?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Documented purpose and scope — intended use and limits through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utili
controls.gap_description: No specific gap details were recorded, but the submission relies on generic, boilerplate language ("documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures") without providing concrete, system-specific evidence that the documented purpose and scope — including intended use cases and explicit limits/exclusions — have been formally defined, approved, and communicated for this general_utility_productivity system at UG assurance level. There is no demonstration that the scope boundaries (e.g., what the system is NOT intended to do, user population limits, operational constraints) are explicitly articulated in a controlled document.
controls.gap_suggestion: 1. Draft or locate a formal Purpose & Scope Statement specific to this system that explicitly defines: (a) the intended use cases, (b) the target user population, (c) operational boundaries and constraints, and (d) out-of-scope uses or prohibited applications. 2. Ensure the document is version-controlled, dated, and approved by the accountable owner. 3. Cross-reference the scope statement with any system design artefacts (e.g., architecture diagrams, data flow diagrams) to confirm alignment. 4. Publish or distribute the scope statement to relevant stakeholders and retain evidence of communication. 5. If responsibilities have been assigned, provide a named RACI or equivalent showing who owns the purpose/scope definition and its maintenance. All artefacts must be system-specific — generic or template-level language will not satisfy the control at UG assurance level.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: System context captured — domain, stakeholders, decision impact, scale
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest's system documentation clearly capture that it operates in a charity kitchen context, that kitchen staff are the primary users, that its decisions influence meal preparation for vulnerable community members, and that it runs as a single-tablet tool suggesting up to three recipes per query using GPT-4o?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses System context captured — domain, stakeholders, decision impact, scale through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for
gaps: No explicit documentation of relevant legal or social norms/expectations applicable to the context (e.g., food safety considerations, community kitchen regulations) as required by MAP 1.1
Organisational risk tolerance is not formally stated or documented (MAP 1.5)

No reference to how external stakeholder feedback (e.g., kitchen visitors, community members) would be collected or integrated, as required by GOVERN 5.1 and 5.2 — though the low-risk, minimal-scale context may make this a minor gap
Alignment with organisational mission or broader goals for AI use is not documented (MAP 1.3)
controls.gap_description: Four interrelated contextual documentation gaps are present for this P2 domain system: (1) No explicit documentation of applicable legal or social norms and expectations for the operational context (e.g., food safety regulations, community kitchen standards) as required by MAP 1.1; (2) Organisational risk tolerance has not been formally stated or documented anywhere in the submission, as required by MAP 1.5; (3) No mechanism or process is described for collecting and integrating external stakeholder feedback (e.g., from kitchen visitors or community members) as required by GOVERN 5.1 and 5.2 — even at a lightweight scale appropriate to the low-risk context; and (4) Alignment between this AI system's use and the organisation's broader mission or strategic goals for AI adoption is absent, as required by MAP 1.3. Together, these gaps mean the system context is only partially captured and lacks the normative, risk, stakeholder, and strategic framing required for a complete MAP/GOVERN baseline.
controls.gap_suggestion: Before the Certifier phase, take the following concrete steps: (1) MAP 1.1 — Produce a short context register (1–2 pages) that explicitly lists applicable legal obligations (e.g., local food safety legislation, community kitchen bylaws, data privacy rules) and relevant social norms or community expectations, and link each to how the system's design accounts for them. (2) MAP 1.5 — Draft and have a responsible owner sign a formal risk tolerance statement that defines acceptable risk thresholds for this system (e.g., acceptable error rates in recommendations, tolerance for downtime), referencing the organisation's broader risk appetite where it exists. (3) GOVERN 5.1 / 5.2 — Define a proportionate external stakeholder feedback mechanism suited to the low-risk, minimal-scale context — this could be as lightweight as a periodic feedback form, a designated point of contact for community members, or a scheduled review meeting — and document how feedback will be reviewed and acted upon. (4) MAP 1.3 — Add a brief mission-alignment statement to the system documentation that explicitly connects this AI system's purpose and intended outcomes to the organisation's stated mission and any organisational AI strategy or principles document.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Risk classification completed — minimal, limited, high, unacceptable
controls.reviewer_question: Has RecipeSuggest been formally classified under the EU AI Act risk tiers — minimal, limited, high, or unacceptable — given its role as a volunteer-built ingredient-to-recipe suggestion tool used by a small UK charity kitchen, and is this classification documented even at a basic level appropriate for an L1 assurance grade?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Risk classification completed — minimal, limited, high, unacceptable through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a
gaps: Residual risk is not explicitly documented — even for minimal-risk systems, NIST AI RMF guidance requires documenting remaining risks after treatment measures, to inform end users
No mention of how or when the classification will be reviewed or reassessed (e.g., if scope, user base, or capabilities change)
The submission does not address what would trigger reclassification to a higher tier (e.g., expansion to public deployment or addition of data collection)
controls.gap_description: Three interrelated deficiencies exist in the risk classification submission for this P2 control: (1) Residual risk is not explicitly documented — even for minimal-risk systems, NIST AI RMF guidance requires that remaining risks after treatment measures are recorded and communicated to end users; (2) There is no documented process or schedule for reviewing or reassessing the risk classification when material changes occur (e.g., changes to scope, user base, or system capabilities); (3) The submission does not define reclassification triggers — specific conditions that would escalate the system to a higher risk tier (e.g., expansion to public deployment, addition of sensitive data collection, or integration with third-party models) are entirely absent.
controls.gap_suggestion: 1. RESIDUAL RISK DOCUMENTATION: Produce a residual risk register or summary statement for the system that explicitly records all risks remaining after treatment controls are applied, their likelihood and impact ratings, and the rationale for accepting them at the current classification tier. This must be present even if the system is classified as minimal-risk, and should be communicated to relevant end users or operators. 2. REVIEW SCHEDULE: Amend the risk classification policy or SOP to include a defined review cadence (e.g., annual review, or review triggered by a material change event). Document who is responsible for initiating and approving the review, and where outcomes are recorded. 3. RECLASSIFICATION TRIGGERS: Define and document a formal list of trigger conditions that would mandate reclassification to a higher tier. Examples must include at minimum: expansion of the user base to the general public, addition of personal or sensitive data collection, changes to automated decision-making scope, integration of new AI components, or regulatory/legal changes. Embed these triggers into the existing risk management SOP and ensure they are linked to the change management process.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Data minimization
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest collect or retain only the ingredient lists necessary to generate recipe suggestions, and is any input data discarded after the suggestions are returned, rather than being stored or logged beyond immediate operational need?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Data minimization through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity system at UG assuranc
gaps: No formal data minimisation policy or procedure document referenced beyond this single control record — a broader privacy framework or policy hierarchy is not evidenced
No mention of how data minimisation principles are reviewed or audited over time (e.g., periodic review cadence)
The written answer references 'planned implementation measures' but the document suggests the system is already operational — this minor inconsistency is unresolved
No reference to staff/volunteer awareness or training on data minimisation practices
controls.gap_description: The submission for Control P4 – Data Minimisation is insufficient across four dimensions: (1) No broader privacy policy framework or policy hierarchy is evidenced — the control record stands alone without reference to an overarching data minimisation policy or procedure document; (2) There is no documented review or audit cadence demonstrating how data minimisation principles are monitored and enforced over time; (3) A material inconsistency exists between the written attestation referencing 'planned implementation measures' and the apparent operational status of the system, which is unresolved and undermines confidence in the control's current effectiveness; (4) There is no evidence of staff or volunteer awareness, training, or communication regarding data minimisation obligations and practices.
controls.gap_suggestion: Before the Certifier phase, the following concrete steps should be taken: (1) Produce or reference an overarching Privacy or Data Minimisation Policy that sits above this control record, clearly establishing the policy hierarchy, scope, and ownership — ensure this document is formally approved and version-controlled; (2) Define and document a periodic review cadence (e.g., annual audit or quarterly review) for data minimisation practices, including who is responsible, what is reviewed, and how findings are recorded and actioned; (3) Resolve the 'planned vs. operational' inconsistency — either update the written attestation to accurately reflect the current operational state of the system with evidence of implemented measures, or clearly document which measures remain pending with a dated implementation roadmap; (4) Provide evidence of staff and volunteer training or awareness activities on data minimisation, such as training completion records, communications, or inclusion of data minimisation obligations in onboarding/induction materials.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Notice and transparency for data subjects
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest display any notice to kitchen staff explaining that the recipe suggestions are generated by an AI system (OpenAI GPT-4o), and are staff aware of this when using the tablet tool?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Notice and transparency for data subjects through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivi
gaps: No documented process for re-notifying volunteers if the system changes (e.g., if a new AI provider is used or new data types are introduced)
No formal acknowledgement or sign-off record from the two volunteers confirming they received and understood the notice
The handbook paragraph is referenced but not reproduced or appended — its exact wording and adequacy cannot be independently verified from this submission alone
No mention of how notice would be updated or communicated if the tool's scope expands to process personal data in the future
controls.gap_description:
Four distinct transparency and notice gaps exist under P4:

1. **Re-notification process absent**: There is no documented process for re-notifying volunteers when material system changes occur — such as the introduction of a new AI provider or the collection of new data types. The submission contains no trigger-based or periodic re-notification workflow.

2. **No acknowledgement or sign-off records**: There are no formal records confirming that the two identified volunteers received, read, and understood the data subject notice. Without signed or logged acknowledgements, there is no verifiable proof that notice was effectively delivered.

3. **Handbook paragraph not reproduced or appended**: The submission references a handbook paragraph as the basis for the notice but does not reproduce or attach its exact wording. The adequacy, completeness, and regulatory sufficiency of that notice cannot be independently assessed from the submission alone.

4. **No future-scope notice update mechanism**: The submission does not describe how the notice would be revised or re-communicated if the tool's scope expands to process personal data in the future, leaving a forward-looking transparency gap.
controls.gap_suggestion:
Address each gap with the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase:

1. **Re-notification process**: Draft and formalise a written procedure that defines specific triggers for re-notification (e.g., change of AI provider, introduction of new data categories, change in data retention periods). The procedure should specify the timeline, responsible role, and communication channel for issuing updated notices to data subjects.

2. **Acknowledgement records**: Collect and retain signed acknowledgement forms — or equivalent logged digital confirmations — from both volunteers confirming receipt and understanding of the current notice. These records must be dated and attributable to named individuals.

3. **Handbook paragraph**: Reproduce the exact text of the referenced handbook paragraph in the submission (or append it as an annex). Conduct a gap analysis against applicable notice requirements (e.g., GDPR Art. 13/14 elements or equivalent) to confirm its adequacy, and update the wording if deficiencies are found.

4. **Future-scope update mechanism**: Add a clause to the notice management procedure that explicitly addresses scope expansion scenarios. This should include a commitment to update the notice prior to any new processing activity commencing, with a defined review and approval workflow and a re-notification obligation to affected data subjects.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Data retention and deletion
controls.reviewer_question: How long does RecipeSuggest retain ingredient lists entered by kitchen staff, and is there a process to delete this data from the tablet and any OpenAI API logs? Does the charity have a documented retention policy covering data sent to third-party AI providers?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Data retention and deletion through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity system at U
gaps: No specific retention periods defined (EU AI Act requires minimum 30 months for training/validation/test data and logs)
No description of actual deletion procedures or schedules
No evidence of data integrity preservation mechanisms for retained datasets
No mention of privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs), de-identification, or data minimization methods as required by NIST AI 100-1
No documentation of how logging and record-keeping are implemented for the AI system's operation
No assigned roles or responsibilities specifically for data retention and deletion oversight
Submission is entirely generic — no system-specific policies, procedures, or controls are described
Only R1 submitted; no supporting documents, policy artifacts, or working system descriptions provided
controls.gap_description:
The submission for Control P4 (Data Retention and Deletion) is entirely generic and provides no system-specific content. The following critical elements are absent:

1. **Retention periods**: No defined retention schedules are documented. The EU AI Act mandates a minimum of 30 months for training, validation, and test data as well as operational logs; no such periods are referenced or applied to this system.
2. **Deletion procedures and schedules**: There is no description of how, when, or by whom data deletion is executed — no workflows, triggers, or automated/manual schedules are defined.
3. **Data integrity mechanisms**: No evidence of controls (e.g., checksums, access controls, immutable storage) that preserve the integrity of retained datasets throughout their retention lifecycle.
4. **Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs) and data minimization**: As required by NIST AI 100-1, there is no mention of de-identification, anonymization, pseudonymization, aggregation, or any other data minimization technique applied to retained data.
5. **Logging and record-keeping implementation**: No documentation exists describing how operational logs are generated, stored, protected, and retained for the AI system — including what events are logged, log formats, and retention durations.
6. **Roles and responsibilities**: No named roles, teams, or individuals are assigned ownership or oversight of data retention and deletion activities (e.g., Data Owner, DPO, MLOps team).
7. **System-specific policies and procedures**: The submission contains no artefacts tailored to this general_utility_productivity system at UG assurance level — no SOPs, data maps, or retention registers are provided.
8. **Supporting evidence**: Only a single written attestation (R1) was submitted. No policy documents, technical configurations, design artefacts, or operational proofs accompany the claim.
controls.gap_suggestion:
Address each gap with the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase:

1. **Define and document retention periods**: Draft a Data Retention Schedule specific to this AI system that explicitly states retention durations for training data, validation data, test data, and operational logs — at minimum 30 months as required by the EU AI Act. Map each data category to its legal/regulatory basis for retention.

2. **Document deletion procedures**: Create a formal Data Deletion SOP that describes the end-to-end deletion workflow: triggers (e.g., retention period expiry, user request), deletion methods (secure erasure standards such as NIST SP 800-88), responsible parties, verification steps, and audit trail requirements. Include a deletion schedule or calendar.

3. **Implement and evidence data integrity controls**: Document the technical mechanisms used to preserve dataset integrity during retention (e.g., cryptographic hashing/checksums, access control lists, write-once storage, backup verification). Provide configuration evidence or technical documentation demonstrating these controls are active.

4. **Adopt and document PETs and data minimization**: Identify all personal or sensitive data retained by the system and document which privacy-enhancing techniques are applied (e.g., anonymization, pseudonymization, differential privacy, aggregation). Reference NIST AI 100-1 alignment explicitly in the policy. Produce a data minimization assessment or privacy impact note.

5. **Document logging and record-keeping implementation**: Produce a Logging Architecture document that specifies: what events are logged (model inputs/outputs, data access, deletions, errors), log format and storage location, access controls on logs, log integrity protections, and the retention period for logs (minimum 30 months per EU AI Act). Provide sample log outputs or configuration files as evidence.

6. **Assign roles and responsibilities**: Update the system's RACI matrix or governance documentation to explicitly assign Data Retention Owner, Data Deletion Executor, and Compliance Oversight roles. Include named individuals or teams and escalation paths.

7. **Replace generic submission with system-specific artefacts**: Rewrite all policy and procedure documents to reference this specific general_utility_productivity system, its data flows, its technology stack, and its UG assurance level obligations. Generic boilerplate is not acceptable at Certifier review.

8. **Submit a full evidence package**: Supplement the R1 attestation with the full set of required evidence types listed below, ensuring each document is version-controlled, dated, and approved by an accountable owner.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Protected groups considered
controls.reviewer_question: Has RecipeSuggest been checked to ensure its recipe suggestions do not systematically exclude or disadvantage people based on protected characteristics, such as cultural or religious dietary practices (e.g., halal, kosher, vegetarian), given the charity serves diverse local residents who may have varying dietary needs rooted in their background or beliefs?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Protected groups considered through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity system at U
gaps: No explicit reference to a periodic review cycle for reassessing protected group considerations as the system or user base evolves
Allergen flagging is described as a system prompt instruction but there is no mention of testing or validation that this instruction reliably functions as intended
No mention of how feedback from affected individuals (e.g. kitchen visitors) could be collected and fed back into the system — relevant to GOVERN 5.1 external engagement requirements
controls.gap_description: Three distinct gaps exist under the 'Protected groups considered' control (P5 domain): (1) There is no documented periodic review cycle specifying how and when protected group considerations will be reassessed as the system evolves or the user base changes — the current submission references planned measures but lacks a defined cadence or trigger-based review mechanism. (2) Allergen flagging, while described as a system prompt instruction, has no accompanying evidence of testing or validation to confirm it reliably and consistently performs as intended across varied inputs and edge cases. (3) There is no documented mechanism for collecting feedback from affected individuals (e.g. kitchen visitors or other end-users from protected groups) and feeding that feedback back into system improvement — a requirement aligned with GOVERN 5.1 external engagement obligations.
controls.gap_suggestion: Address each gap as follows before the Certifier phase: (1) REVIEW CYCLE — Draft and approve a formal policy or SOP that defines a periodic review schedule (e.g. semi-annual or triggered by material system changes or user base shifts) for reassessing protected group considerations, including named responsible roles and escalation paths. (2) ALLERGEN FLAGGING VALIDATION — Design and execute a structured test plan covering representative and edge-case prompts to validate that the allergen-flagging system prompt instruction performs reliably; document pass/fail results, failure modes, and any remediation taken. (3) FEEDBACK MECHANISM — Define and document a feedback collection process for affected individuals (e.g. a structured feedback form, periodic user interviews, or a designated reporting channel), including how feedback is reviewed, triaged, and incorporated into system updates; provide evidence that this process is operational or formally planned with an activation date.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Bias testing plan — metrics and datasets
controls.reviewer_question: What metrics and datasets, if any, will you use to test whether RecipeSuggest's recipe suggestions show bias toward or against particular dietary needs, cultural food traditions, or ingredient combinations commonly associated with specific communities served by Nourish Community Kitchen?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Bias testing plan — metrics and datasets through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivit
gaps: No defined metrics are documented — the control explicitly requires 'metrics and datasets' for bias testing; qualitative volunteer impressions do not constitute measurable bias metrics (e.g., no distribution tracking, no cuisine-category counts, no diversity ratio).
No dataset or data sample is identified or referenced — even for a lightweight tool, the ingredients or recipe corpus used should be characterised for representativeness.
The threshold for intervention ('repeatedly inappropriate over two weeks') is subjective and not operationalised — no frequency count, severity scale, or logging mechanism is described.

No documentation of how volunteer assessments are recorded or retained, making independent verification impossible and creating a gap against OECD transparency and NIST MEASURE 2.1 (test sets and tools documented).

The plan does not address intersectional or demographic bias dimensions beyond cuisine geography — e.g., dietary restrictions linked to cultural or religious identity, accessibility of ingredients by socioeconomic context.
NIST MEASURE 2.11 requires fairness and bias evaluation results to be documented; the current plan describes a process but contains no results, even preliminary ones.
EU AI Act Article 19 requires 'documented methods for bias mitigation' — the system prompt adjustment is mentioned but not described as a method with any structured documentation.
controls.gap_description: The submission contains no quantitative bias metrics, no characterised dataset or corpus, no operationalised intervention thresholds, no documented volunteer assessment records, no intersectional bias analysis beyond cuisine geography, no preliminary bias evaluation results, and no structured documentation of bias mitigation methods. The current approach relies entirely on qualitative volunteer impressions and a subjective, unlogged intervention trigger ('repeatedly inappropriate over two weeks'), which fails to satisfy the explicit 'metrics and datasets' requirement of the control, NIST MEASURE 2.1 (test sets and tools documented), NIST MEASURE 2.11 (fairness and bias evaluation results documented), and EU AI Act Article 19 (documented bias mitigation methods). There is no evidence that volunteer assessments are recorded or retained in any form that would permit independent verification.
controls.gap_suggestion:
1. DEFINE QUANTITATIVE BIAS METRICS: Document a minimum metric set covering at least: (a) cuisine-category distribution ratios across all outputs sampled, (b) ingredient diversity index (e.g., Shannon entropy across cultural food groups), (c) representation frequency counts per cuisine/dietary category, and (d) a severity scale (e.g., 1–5) for flagged outputs. Record these in a Bias Testing Metrics Register.

2. CHARACTERISE THE DATASET/CORPUS: Produce a Data Sheet or Model Card section that describes the ingredients/recipe corpus used — including size, source(s), cultural coverage, language(s), and known gaps — so representativeness can be independently assessed.

3. OPERATIONALISE THE INTERVENTION THRESHOLD: Replace the subjective 'repeatedly inappropriate over two weeks' trigger with a defined rule, e.g., '≥3 severity-4+ flags within any rolling 14-day window triggers a mandatory system prompt review'. Document this rule in a Bias Response SOP.

4. IMPLEMENT VOLUNTEER ASSESSMENT LOGGING: Create a structured logging template (digital or paper) capturing: tester ID/role, date, output sampled, metric scores assigned, and free-text notes. Retain logs for a minimum period (e.g., 12 months) to enable independent verification.

5. EXPAND BIAS DIMENSIONS: Extend the testing plan to explicitly address intersectional bias dimensions including: dietary restrictions linked to cultural/religious identity (e.g., halal, kosher, Hindu vegetarian), socioeconomic accessibility of ingredients (e.g., cost proxies, availability by region), and accessibility needs. Document these dimensions in the plan.

6. PRODUCE PRELIMINARY BIAS EVALUATION RESULTS: Run at least one documented bias evaluation cycle using the defined metrics and dataset before the Certifier phase. Record results — even if the system is low-risk — in a Bias Evaluation Results Report to satisfy NIST MEASURE 2.11.

7. DOCUMENT BIAS MITIGATION METHODS: Formalise the system prompt adjustment approach as a structured mitigation method: describe the trigger conditions, the review process, who approves changes, how changes are version-controlled, and how effectiveness is re-evaluated post-adjustment. This satisfies EU AI Act Article 19.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: User recourse and appeals
controls.reviewer_question: If RecipeSuggest suggests recipes that kitchen staff consider unsuitable or impractical given their actual ingredients or dietary requirements of meal recipients, what process exists for staff to flag this, override the suggestions, and request alternative options?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses User recourse and appeals through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity system at UG
gaps: No documented timeframe or expectation for how quickly Sam Okafor will respond to a raised concern, even informally.
No record-keeping or logging mechanism mentioned for concerns raised, which could make it difficult to identify recurring issues over time.
controls.gap_description: No documented timeframe or expectation for how quickly Sam Okafor will respond to a raised concern, even informally. Additionally, there is no record-keeping or logging mechanism mentioned for concerns raised, which could make it difficult to identify recurring issues over time.
controls.gap_suggestion: 1. Define and document a formal or informal response timeframe (e.g., acknowledgement within 2 business days, resolution within 10 business days) for concerns raised through the user recourse and appeals process, and assign this expectation explicitly to Sam Okafor's role. 2. Establish a lightweight logging or record-keeping mechanism (e.g., a shared register, ticketing system, or structured log) to capture all concerns raised, their status, and outcomes. This log should be reviewed periodically to identify recurring issues and inform system improvements. Both measures should be reflected in updated policy or SOP documentation before the Certifier phase.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: User-facing disclosure — AI involvement disclosed
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest clearly inform kitchen staff using the tablet that recipe suggestions are generated by an AI system (specifically GPT-4o), rather than a human or pre-written database, so they understand the nature of the tool they are relying on when preparing meals for community members?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses User-facing disclosure — AI involvement disclosed through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_pr
gaps: No documented process for updating or re-issuing disclosure if the underlying model or system changes (e.g., if GPT-4o is replaced)
Volunteer briefing is informal and undocumented — no sign-off, acknowledgement record, or onboarding checklist to evidence that disclosure was received
No mechanism described for disclosing AI involvement to new or temporary volunteers who join after the initial briefing by Sam Okafor
No reference to how users can seek further information or challenge AI outputs, as required by OECD Principle 1.30(iv) and EU AI Act Article 35
controls.gap_description: Four distinct deficiencies undermine this control's readiness: (1) There is no documented process governing how and when disclosure notices are reviewed, updated, or re-issued when the underlying AI model or system changes (e.g., a transition from GPT-4o to a successor model), meaning disclosures may become stale and inaccurate without any trigger or owner. (2) Volunteer briefings on AI involvement are conducted informally by Sam Okafor with no sign-off sheet, acknowledgement record, or onboarding checklist — there is currently no auditable evidence that any individual volunteer received and understood the disclosure. (3) There is no described mechanism to ensure new or temporary volunteers who join after the initial briefing cohort are briefed on AI involvement, creating a structural gap where an entire class of users may operate the system without ever receiving disclosure. (4) The submission contains no reference to a user-facing channel or procedure through which users can seek further information about the AI system or challenge AI-generated outputs, as explicitly required by OECD Principle 1.30(iv) and EU AI Act Article 35.
controls.gap_suggestion: Before the Certifier phase, take the following concrete steps: (1) Draft and adopt a Model/System Change Disclosure SOP that defines a trigger list (e.g., model version change, provider change, material capability change), assigns a named owner responsible for reviewing and re-issuing disclosure notices within a defined SLA (e.g., 5 business days of change), and records each re-issuance event in a disclosure change log. (2) Create a formal volunteer onboarding checklist that includes an AI-disclosure acknowledgement item; require each volunteer (existing and new) to sign or digitally acknowledge receipt — retain these records in a centralised register. Backfill acknowledgements for all volunteers briefed to date by Sam Okafor. (3) Embed the AI-disclosure briefing and acknowledgement step into the standard onboarding workflow for all new and temporary volunteers, so that no individual can be granted system access before disclosure is confirmed and logged. (4) Add a clearly visible 'AI Information & Challenge' section to all user-facing interfaces and documentation, specifying: (a) a named contact or helpdesk channel for further questions about the AI system, (b) a described process by which users can flag, contest, or request human review of AI outputs, and (c) a reference to the applicable regulatory basis (OECD Principle 1.30(iv); EU AI Act Article 35). Document this mechanism in the system's transparency policy.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: System limitations stated — known failure modes
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest's documentation or interface clearly communicate to kitchen staff its known limitations — such as potential ingredient mismatches, inability to account for allergens or dietary restrictions, possible hallucinated recipes, and the risk of suggesting dishes requiring unavailable equipment or techniques — so staff can confidently verify suggestions before preparing meals?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses System limitations stated — known failure modes through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_prod
gaps: No formal process described for updating or reviewing the stated limitations over time as the system evolves
No mechanism documented for users to report newly discovered failure modes or edge cases back to the system owner
Limitations are stated informally without reference to any structured risk register or failure mode analysis, which may be expected at higher assurance levels (not critical at UG)
controls.gap_description: Three interrelated weaknesses undermine full readiness for this control: (1) There is no formal, recurring process for reviewing and updating the stated system limitations as the system evolves — the current documentation captures a point-in-time snapshot with no defined review cadence or trigger conditions. (2) There is no documented mechanism by which users can report newly discovered failure modes or edge cases back to the system owner, meaning the feedback loop between operational experience and stated limitations is absent. (3) The limitations are expressed informally in narrative prose with no traceable link to a structured failure mode analysis (e.g., FMEA, risk register, or equivalent artefact), leaving the basis for the stated limitations unverifiable by a Certifier.
controls.gap_suggestion:
1. REVIEW PROCESS — Draft and adopt a short Limitations Review SOP (or add a dedicated section to an existing policy) that specifies: (a) a minimum annual review cycle, (b) event-triggered reviews (e.g., new model version, significant change in use-case scope, post-incident), and (c) named role(s) responsible for initiating and approving each review. Record the next scheduled review date in the document itself.

2. USER FEEDBACK MECHANISM — Document a lightweight, named channel through which users can submit reports of unexpected behaviour or newly discovered failure modes (e.g., a dedicated email alias, a ticketing queue, or a feedback form). Publish this channel in the user-facing limitations statement and define the triage/response SLA in the SOP. Retain logs of submissions and dispositions as operational proof.

3. STRUCTURED FAILURE MODE ANALYSIS — Produce or reference a structured artefact (risk register entry, FMEA table, or equivalent) that lists each known failure mode, its likelihood/impact rating, and the mitigating control or caveat already stated to users. Cross-reference this artefact from the limitations statement so a Certifier can trace each stated limitation back to its analytical basis. At UG assurance level a lightweight table is sufficient — exhaustive quantitative analysis is not required.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Explainability appropriate to context
controls.reviewer_question: How does RecipeSuggest communicate to kitchen staff why particular recipes have been suggested for the available ingredients, and is this level of explanation sufficient for staff to confidently act on or override the tool's suggestions?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Explainability appropriate to context through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity s
gaps: No documented mechanism for how the system prompt instruction is maintained or reviewed over time — if the prompt changes, the explainability commitment could silently degrade.
No mention of what happens if a volunteer does not understand or disputes a suggestion — there is no described recourse or challenge pathway, which is referenced in OECD 1.30 (iv).

The document does not address explainability to end-beneficiaries (e.g., community kitchen guests) if they were ever to interact with or be affected by the system's outputs, though this may be out of scope for the current deployment context.
controls.gap_description: Three distinct explainability gaps exist under P6: (1) There is no documented mechanism governing how the system prompt instruction is maintained or reviewed over time — meaning any change to the prompt could silently erode the explainability commitment without detection or accountability. (2) There is no described recourse or challenge pathway for volunteers who do not understand or wish to dispute a system suggestion, as required by OECD 1.30(iv). (3) The submission does not address explainability obligations toward end-beneficiaries (e.g., community kitchen guests) who may be indirectly affected by the system's outputs, leaving a potential gap if the deployment context expands.
controls.gap_suggestion: Address all three gaps before the Certifier phase as follows: (1) Prompt governance — establish and document a formal prompt change-management process, including version control for the system prompt, a designated reviewer/owner, a defined review cadence (e.g., quarterly or on material change), and a sign-off record confirming that explainability commitments are re-validated after each change. (2) Recourse pathway — document a clear, accessible process by which a volunteer can flag that they do not understand a suggestion or wish to challenge it, including who receives the challenge, the expected response timeframe, and how outcomes are recorded; reference this pathway explicitly in volunteer-facing materials. (3) End-beneficiary explainability — either formally document that end-beneficiaries are out of scope for the current deployment context (with a rationale and boundary conditions that would trigger a re-assessment), or, if they may be affected, draft a plain-language explainability statement describing what the system does and how it influences decisions that affect them.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Documentation completeness — model card and datasheet
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest have basic documentation covering its purpose (ingredient-based recipe suggestions for kitchen staff), the GPT-4o model it relies on, known limitations such as potential ingredient mismatches or unsuitable recipes, and guidance for the volunteer maintainer? Given the L1 assurance grade, is this documentation proportionate and sufficient for a small charity tool, even if a full model card isn't required?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Documentation completeness — model card and datasheet through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utilit
gaps: No datasheet is provided — the submission includes a model card but the control explicitly references both a model card and a datasheet; a datasheet would typically cover training data characteristics in more depth, though this is partially mitigated by the API/no-fine-tuning context
Testing and evaluation procedures are not described (e.g., how the system prompt was validated, any informal testing done before deployment)
No description of the system prompt content or how kitchen-specific instructions were determined
Performance metrics or any form of output quality assessment are absent
controls.gap_description: The submission provides only a model card and lacks four key documentation elements required by this control: (1) a datasheet covering training data characteristics (partially mitigated by the API/no-fine-tuning context, but still absent as a discrete artefact); (2) any description of testing and evaluation procedures, including how the system prompt was validated or what informal pre-deployment testing was conducted; (3) a description of the system prompt content and the rationale for how kitchen-specific instructions were determined; and (4) performance metrics or output quality assessment of any kind. The current submission text is generic boilerplate and does not demonstrate substantive engagement with any of these documentation requirements.
controls.gap_suggestion: 1. DATASHEET: Produce a datasheet artefact (even a concise one) that documents the upstream model's training data provenance, known data characteristics, and any limitations relevant to the kitchen/utility context. Reference the API provider's published model documentation (e.g., OpenAI model cards, Anthropic model cards) and explicitly link it to this submission to partially satisfy the training-data dimension in a no-fine-tuning context. 2. TESTING & EVALUATION: Document the testing and evaluation procedures applied before deployment — at minimum, describe any informal prompt testing, scenario walkthroughs, or user acceptance checks performed. Record who conducted the testing, when, and what criteria were used to judge acceptability. 3. SYSTEM PROMPT: Provide a description (or redacted summary if confidentiality is a concern) of the system prompt content, explain the process by which kitchen-specific instructions were identified and drafted, and record who approved the final prompt. 4. PERFORMANCE METRICS: Define and document at least a basic output quality assessment — this could be a structured set of test cases with expected vs. actual outputs, user feedback collected post-deployment, or qualitative evaluation criteria. Compile these into the model card or a supplementary evaluation report and attach as evidence.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: AI identity non-deception
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest clearly identify itself as an AI-powered tool to kitchen staff who interact with it, and does it avoid creating any impression that recipe suggestions come from a human source or carry authoritative nutritional or dietary endorsement beyond what the system is designed to provide?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses AI identity non-deception through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity system at UG
gaps: No documented process for periodic re-testing or ongoing monitoring to ensure the non-deception instruction persists through model or system prompt updates
No formal policy document beyond the system prompt instruction — a brief written policy or procedure referencing this control would strengthen auditability
No mention of how the control is maintained if the underlying model (GPT-4o) or system prompt is changed by an administrator
controls.gap_description: Three interrelated deficiencies undermine the completeness of this control: (1) There is no documented process for periodic re-testing or ongoing monitoring to verify that the non-deception instruction survives model or system prompt updates — the current posture relies solely on a static system prompt with no assurance it persists after changes. (2) There is no standalone formal policy or procedure document governing AI identity non-deception; the system prompt instruction alone is insufficient for auditability, as it conflates the control mechanism with the control governance. (3) There is no defined change-management or continuity procedure specifying how the control is validated and reinstated when the underlying model (e.g., GPT-4o) or system prompt is modified by an administrator — leaving a potential window of non-compliance after every update.
controls.gap_suggestion: 1. POLICY DOCUMENT: Draft and approve a concise formal policy (1–2 pages) explicitly governing AI identity non-deception for this system. It should state the requirement, scope, owner, review cadence, and reference the system prompt as the primary technical control mechanism. 2. CHANGE MANAGEMENT PROCEDURE: Create a documented SOP that mandates a non-deception verification step as part of any model upgrade or system prompt change workflow. This should include a named responsible role (e.g., System Administrator or AI Product Owner), a required sign-off checklist, and a maximum allowable time-to-verify window after each change. 3. PERIODIC RE-TESTING PLAN: Define and implement a scheduled re-testing regime (e.g., quarterly or after every model/prompt update) using a standardised set of probe questions designed to confirm the AI correctly identifies itself and does not deceive users about its nature. Log results and retain them as operational evidence. 4. MONITORING LOGS: Where technically feasible, enable or configure logging of interactions where AI identity is queried, to support ongoing assurance and incident detection. Ensure logs are retained in line with the organisation's data retention policy.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Safety requirements defined — harm scenarios
controls.reviewer_question: Has RecipeSuggest identified potential harm scenarios specific to its use, such as suggesting recipes containing allergens not flagged by staff, recommending unsafe ingredient combinations, or providing inaccurate cooking instructions that could affect the health of vulnerable meal recipients at Nourish Community Kitchen?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Safety requirements defined — harm scenarios through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_product
gaps: No explicit reference to a process for reviewing or updating harm scenarios over time (e.g., periodic review cadence)
Volunteer over-reliance scenario mitigation ('limitations clearly stated') lacks detail on where/how this is communicated beyond the system prompt
No documented incident reporting pathway beyond 'report to Sam' for the offensive content scenario
controls.gap_description: Three distinct deficiencies exist in the harm scenario documentation for this P7 control: (1) There is no defined process or cadence for periodically reviewing and updating harm scenarios — the submission contains no schedule, trigger conditions, or ownership for revisiting scenarios as the system evolves or new risks emerge. (2) The mitigation for the volunteer over-reliance scenario ('limitations clearly stated') is insufficiently detailed — it is unclear where these limitations are surfaced beyond the system prompt (e.g., UI disclosures, onboarding materials, in-context warnings), and there is no evidence of how their effectiveness is monitored. (3) The incident reporting pathway for the offensive content scenario is underdocumented — 'report to Sam' does not constitute a formal pathway; there is no named role/title, escalation chain, response SLA, or record-keeping mechanism described.
controls.gap_suggestion: Address each gap as follows before the Certifier phase: (1) PERIODIC REVIEW PROCESS — Draft and approve a short SOP or policy addendum that specifies: a named review owner (by role, not individual), a minimum review cadence (e.g., annually or upon material system change), and the criteria that trigger an out-of-cycle review. Record the date of the most recent review. (2) OVER-RELIANCE LIMITATION COMMUNICATIONS — Enumerate every touchpoint where volunteer limitations are disclosed (e.g., system prompt, UI tooltip, onboarding screen, help documentation) and provide screenshots or design artefacts for each. Add a brief statement on how the adequacy of these disclosures is assessed (e.g., user testing, feedback review). (3) INCIDENT REPORTING PATHWAY — Replace the informal 'report to Sam' reference with a documented incident response procedure that includes: a role-based contact (e.g., 'AI Safety Lead'), an alternative/backup contact, a defined response SLA, a log or ticketing mechanism for tracking reports, and a feedback loop to harm scenario updates. A simple one-page SOP or RACI entry is sufficient at UG assurance level.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: System description pack complete
controls.reviewer_question: Has the system description pack for RecipeSuggest been completed, including documentation of the GPT-4o API integration, the ingredient-to-recipe suggestion workflow, the single-tablet deployment setup, and the volunteer-built context within Nourish Community Kitchen's charitable operations?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses System description pack complete through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity system
gaps: No explicit mapping to the OECD AI System definition or other regulatory framework cited in the control context — a brief statement acknowledging the system meets the definition of an AI system would strengthen traceability
No description of the system prompt content beyond a high-level summary — the actual prompt or its key constraints are not reproduced or referenced
No mention of how the zero-retention API option is verified or audited over time
Assurance level (UG) is referenced in the written answer but not explained or justified within the document itself
controls.gap_description: Four distinct deficiencies exist in the system description pack: (1) No explicit mapping or acknowledgement that the system meets the OECD AI System definition (or equivalent regulatory framework cited in the control context), leaving traceability incomplete. (2) The system prompt content is only summarised at a high level — the actual prompt text or its key constraints (e.g. scope limitations, safety guardrails, persona boundaries) are neither reproduced nor formally referenced. (3) There is no documented mechanism, verification procedure, or audit trail confirming that the zero-retention API option is active and remains enforced over time. (4) The UG assurance level is cited in the written answer but is not explained, justified, or cross-referenced within the system description pack itself, making the rationale opaque to reviewers and certifiers.
controls.gap_suggestion:
Close all four gaps before the Certifier phase as follows:
1. OECD/Regulatory Mapping — Add a dedicated paragraph (or annex) to the system description pack that explicitly references the applicable regulatory definition of an AI system (e.g. OECD AI Principles, EU AI Act Article 3(1), or the framework cited in the control context) and includes a brief statement confirming the system satisfies that definition, with a rationale sentence linking system characteristics to each definitional criterion.
2. System Prompt Documentation — Append the full system prompt text (or a formally version-controlled excerpt covering all key constraints) as a controlled annex to the pack. If the prompt is commercially sensitive, produce a redacted reference copy and log the full version in a restricted evidence repository, cross-referencing it from the pack.
3. Zero-Retention Verification — Document the technical mechanism used to enable zero-retention (e.g. API header/flag, contractual data-processing addendum clause) and establish a periodic verification procedure (e.g. quarterly log review or automated header-check test) with results recorded in an audit log. Include at least one completed verification record as evidence.
4. UG Assurance Level Justification — Insert a clearly labelled section in the system description pack that defines the UG assurance level, explains the criteria used to assign it to this system (e.g. risk tier, user population, data sensitivity), and cross-references the assurance framework document from which the level is drawn.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Accessibility requirements captured
controls.reviewer_question: Does RecipeSuggest meet accessibility needs for all kitchen staff who may use the tablet, including those with visual impairments, dyslexia, or limited digital literacy, ensuring the ingredient input and recipe display functions are usable by everyone who volunteers or works at Nourish Community Kitchen?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Accessibility requirements captured through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity sys
gaps: No formal review cycle or trigger documented beyond 'if volunteers change' — a periodic review cadence would strengthen ongoing compliance
Language accessibility is noted as English-only with no documented process for assessing non-English-speaking volunteers beyond a general 'reviewed if volunteers change' note
No reference to any recognised accessibility standard (e.g., WCAG) even at a basic level, which may be expected at UG assurance level for completeness
controls.gap_description: Three distinct deficiencies exist in the current accessibility requirements documentation for this P10 control: (1) There is no formal, periodic review cadence defined — the only documented trigger for revisiting accessibility requirements is 'if volunteers change', which is event-driven and ad hoc rather than a structured, time-bound cycle. (2) Language accessibility for non-English-speaking volunteers is unaddressed — there is no documented process for identifying, assessing, or accommodating volunteers whose primary language is not English, beyond the same vague 'reviewed if volunteers change' note. (3) There is no reference to any recognised accessibility standard (e.g., WCAG 2.1 or equivalent) in the policy or design artefacts, which is expected for completeness at UG assurance level for a general utility/productivity system.
controls.gap_suggestion: Take the following concrete steps before the Certifier phase: (1) REVIEW CADENCE — Amend the existing accessibility policy or SOP to define an explicit periodic review cycle (e.g., annually or bi-annually), document the review trigger criteria (including but not limited to volunteer changes), and name the role responsible for initiating each review. Retain dated meeting minutes or a review log as evidence. (2) LANGUAGE ACCESSIBILITY PROCESS — Draft and formalise a short process or procedure that describes how the organisation identifies non-English-speaking volunteers at onboarding, what assessment or accommodation steps are taken (e.g., translated materials, bilingual support), and how this is recorded. This can be a lightweight addendum to the existing accessibility policy. (3) ACCESSIBILITY STANDARD REFERENCE — Update the policy, design documentation, or requirements register to explicitly reference a recognised accessibility standard appropriate to the system's scope (e.g., WCAG 2.1 Level A/AA for any user-facing interfaces, or an equivalent standard for non-web tooling). A brief rationale statement explaining the chosen standard and its applicability to the system is sufficient for UG assurance level.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

controls.title: Intended societal benefit articulated
controls.reviewer_question: Has the volunteer or Nourish Community Kitchen clearly articulated how RecipeSuggest benefits the charity's mission — for example, by reducing food waste, saving staff time, or helping provide more varied meals to local residents?
controls.submission_summary: This system addresses Intended societal benefit articulated through documented policies, assigned responsibilities, and planned implementation measures appropriate for a general_utility_productivity s
gaps: No explicit linkage to any recognised framework or standard for societal benefit articulation (e.g., ATRS or equivalent), though this is not strictly required at this assurance level
Benefit recognition relies solely on informal observation by one individual (Sam Okafor); even a lightweight qualitative indicator or periodic check-in cadence would strengthen ongoing accountability
controls.gap_description: Two weaknesses undermine the current articulation of intended societal benefit: (1) The benefit claim is not anchored to any recognised external framework or standard (e.g., ATRS or equivalent), leaving the articulation without an independently verifiable reference point. While not strictly mandatory at UG assurance level, the absence reduces credibility and comparability. (2) Ongoing recognition and monitoring of societal benefit rests entirely on informal, single-person observation by Sam Okafor, with no lightweight qualitative indicator, structured check-in cadence, or secondary accountability mechanism in place. This creates a single point of failure for continued benefit accountability and provides no auditable trail of periodic review.
controls.gap_suggestion: 1. Framework linkage: Annotate the existing benefit articulation document to map the stated societal benefits to at least one recognised reference point (e.g., ATRS societal benefit categories, UN SDGs, or an equivalent domain-relevant standard). Even a brief mapping table appended to the current policy document is sufficient at UG level. 2. Lightweight monitoring cadence: Establish a simple, repeatable check-in process — for example, a quarterly one-page qualitative review completed by Sam Okafor and countersigned by a second responsible party (e.g., a line manager or product owner). Define at least one qualitative indicator (e.g., user-reported utility, accessibility reach, or harm-reduction signal) to track benefit realisation over time. Document the cadence formally in the relevant policy or SOP, and retain completed review records as operational proof. Both actions should be completed and evidenced before the Certifier phase review.
controls.commitment_text: We commit to addressing the identified gaps before the Certifier phase through targeted implementation and documentation.

critical_gaps.gap: No specific retention periods defined (EU AI Act requires minimum 30 months for training/validation/test data and logs)
No description of actual deletion procedures or schedules
No evidence of data integrity preservation mechanisms for retained datasets
No mention of privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs), de-identification, or data minimization methods as required by NIST AI 100-1
No documentation of how logging and record-keeping are implemented for the AI system's operation
No assigned roles or responsibilities specifically for data retention and deletion oversight
Submission is entirely generic — no system-specific policies, procedures, or controls are described
Only R1 submitted; no supporting documents, policy artifacts, or working system descriptions provided
